mainTopic: What a craftsman or worker may keep from a customer's materials, and what may be bought from him, closing מסכת בבא קמא.
overview: This amud finishes the last פרק of בבא קמא, which deals with what a craftsman may keep from a customer's materials. The גמרא first explains a ברייתא about a carder and a launderer. It settles apparent contradictions by splitting the cases: thick versus thin threads, an ordinary garment versus a fine cape, and a garment versus a belt. רבי ירמיה's question about how to count stitches ends in תיקו. Next come ברייתות about buying from a carder, a weaver, and a dyer. Raw leftovers may not be bought, but items the craftsman changed may be bought, because he acquired them through שינוי. The גמרא then works through the rest of the משנה: the launderer's short threads, the tailor's leftover thread (proved to mean two needle-lengths), and a carpenter's chips (where רבא explains that the word מעצד meant different tools in different places). It ends with workers' scraps and wild plants, where it all depends on whether the owner, or the local people, care. The מסכת closes with the הדרן.

steps.title: End of the ברייתא: stitches, carding direction, and trimming
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives rules for a craftsman working on someone else's cloth: no more than three stitches, card along the weft, and trim only along the length unless it is up to a טפח.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he should not put more than three stitches into it. He should not card the garment along its warp, only along its weft. He may even it out along its length, but not along its width. And if he wants to even it out by up to a טפח, he is allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: We are reading the end of a ברייתא that lists what a craftsman may and may not do to a customer's cloth. The גמרא will ask questions on these lines in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each rule protects the cloth's owner from damage: too many stitches overstretch the fabric, and carding the wrong way wears it out. Trimming is limited to the length. The last line makes one exception: trimming up to a טפח is fine.

keyTerms.meaning: Stitches used to hold the cloth while it is stretched
To card or comb the cloth to raise its fibers
The warp, the threads running lengthwise
The weft, the threads running crosswise
A teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה

phrases.english: And he should not place in it
more than three stitches,
and he should not card the garment along its warp
phrases.notes: Warp means the threads that run lengthwise. Weft, in the next row, means the threads that run across.

phrases.english: but rather along its weft.
And he may even it out along its length,
but not along its width.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם בָּא לְהַשְׁווֹתוֹ עַד טֶפַח – רַשַּׁאי.
phrases.english: And if he comes to even it out up to a handbreadth, he is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא יָטִיל בּוֹ יוֹתֵר מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה חוּבִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a ברייתא that started before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Use no more than three stitches. Card along the weft, not the warp. Trim along the length, not the width, but trimming up to a טפח is allowed.

steps.title: Two threads or three?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says the launderer may keep two threads, but the משנה says three.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said in the ברייתא: two threads. But we learned in the משנה: three!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to an earlier line of the ברייתא and points out that it seems to contradict the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier part of the ברייתא let the כובס keep two threads. Our משנה gives him three. The two sources seem to disagree on the same rule.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said: the גמרא is quoting a line from the ברייתא
But didn't we learn in the משנה?

phrases.english: The Master said: two threads.
phrases.notes: This quotes an earlier line of the same ברייתא, which let the launderer keep two threads.

phrases.english: But didn't we learn: three!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts examining the ברייתא by comparing it with the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling of two threads
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה allows three threads, so the ברייתא seems to contradict it.

steps.title: Thick threads versus thin threads
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's two threads refers to thick threads. The משנה's three threads refers to thin ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: this one is about thick threads, and that one is about thin threads.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two sources are not arguing. They are describing different kinds of thread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Thick threads take away more material, so the launderer may keep only two. Thin threads take away less, so he may keep three. The limit depends on how much material is lost.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; the question is answered

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this one is with thick ones,
phrases.notes: This one means the ברייתא, which allows two threads.

phrases.english: and that one is with thin ones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction from step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the sources into two different cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought both sources were talking about the same threads.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two thick threads or three thin threads.

steps.title: Another ברייתא says the opposite about carding
steps.stepSummary: Our ברייתא says to card along the weft, not the warp, but another ברייתא says the opposite.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he should not card the garment along its warp, only along its weft. But it is taught in another ברייתא the opposite!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the carding rule again and challenges it with a different ברייתא that says the reverse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two ברייתות give opposite directions for carding. The question is which way the craftsman is really supposed to card.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא?

phrases.english: And he should not card the garment along its warp,
but rather along its weft.
But isn't it taught the opposite!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next line of the ברייתא and raises a new contradiction.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule to card only along the weft
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another ברייתא tells the craftsman to card the other way.

steps.title: Ordinary garment versus elegant cape
steps.stepSummary: Our ברייתא is about an ordinary garment. The other ברייתא is about an elegant cape.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: this one is about an ordinary garment, and that one is about an elegant cape.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two ברייתות are about different kinds of clothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ordinary garment needs to last, so carding along the warp, which wears it out, is not allowed. An elegant cape is made to look nice, and carding along the warp improves its appearance. The correct direction depends on what the garment is for.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this one is with an ordinary garment,
that one is with an elegant cape.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction from step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the sources into two different cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought both ברייתות were about the same kind of garment.
steps.terutzMaskana: Card an ordinary garment along the weft. A fine cape may be carded along the warp.

steps.title: What counts as one stitch?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks whether one in-and-out pass of the needle counts as one stitch or two.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he should not put more than three stitches into it. רבי ירמיה asked: Does taking the needle in and out count as one stitch, or perhaps in and out counts as two?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the stitch rule from the ברייתא again, and רבי ירמיה asks how stitches are counted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא limits the craftsman to three stitches, but it does not say what a single stitch is. If in and out together is one stitch, he may make more passes of the needle. If in and out is two, he may make fewer.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked a question that has no obvious answer

phrases.english: And he should not place in it
more than three stitches.
Rabbi Yirmeya asked:
Taking in and bringing out: is it one,
phrases.notes: He means pushing the needle into the cloth and pulling it back out.

phrases.english: or perhaps taking in and bringing out is two?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to another line of the ברייתא to define one of its words.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does one in-and-out pass of the needle count as one stitch or two?

steps.title: The question is left open
steps.stepSummary: The question about counting stitches is not answered.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends רבי ירמיה's question with תיקו, meaning no answer was found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source settles whether in and out is one stitch or two. The question stays unanswered.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question remains unanswered

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's rules are explained by splitting the cases. Two thick threads or three thin threads. An ordinary garment is carded along the weft, while a fine cape may be carded along the warp. How to count stitches is left as תיקו.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes רבי ירמיה's question without answering it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: It is not decided whether in and out counts as one stitch or two.

steps.title: Evening out the cloth along its length, not its width
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: the craftsman may even out the cloth along its length but not along its width.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he may even it out along its length, but not along its width.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes again the trimming line of the ברייתא from step 1, so it can challenge it. This is not a new rule; it sets up the contradiction in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The craftsman may straighten the uneven edge of the cloth along its length. He may not do it along its width. This sets up the contradiction in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: He evens it out, makes it straight

phrases.english: And he may even it out along its length
but not along its width.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the ברייתא discussed in earlier steps, after the unanswered question of רבי ירמיה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The cloth may be evened out along its length but not along its width.

steps.title: Another ברייתא says the opposite
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא rules the reverse: even out the width, not the length.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't it taught the opposite?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rule it just quoted. It points to a different ברייתא that says the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One ברייתא says length, the other says width. Both cannot be true about the same case, so the גמרא needs to explain the clash.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it taught (in a ברייתא)?

phrases.english: But isn't it taught the opposite!
phrases.notes: The other ברייתא says to even it out along the width and not the length.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the rule of step 8 with a contradicting ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that one evens out the length and not the width.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two ברייתות give opposite rules for the same action.

steps.title: A garment versus a belt
steps.stepSummary: Each ברייתא is talking about a different item: one about a regular garment, the other about a belt.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: this one is about a garment, that one is about a belt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the contradiction. Each ברייתא is talking about a different kind of item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a גלימא (garment), you even out the length. For a המיוני (belt), you even out the width. The two ברייתות do not argue; they describe different objects.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction

steps.confusionAlert: This is a different contradiction from steps 4–5. That one was about carding along the warp or the weft. This one is about evening out the length or the width.

phrases.english: It is not difficult: this one is about a garment,
phrases.notes: "This one" is our ברייתא, which says to even out the length.

phrases.english: that one is about a belt.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא; הָא בִּגְלִימָא, הָא בְּהֶמְיוֹנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 9.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות discuss the same item and argue.
steps.terutzMaskana: A garment is evened out along its length; a belt along its width.

steps.title: Buying strands from a carder
steps.stepSummary: Do not buy loose strands from a סורק (carder), since they probably belong to the customer. Where local custom lets him keep them, you may buy them. A finished cushion or mattress stuffed with strands may be bought anywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: One may not buy strands from a carder, because they are not his. In a place where the custom is that they are his, one may buy them. And everywhere, one may buy from them a cushion full of strands or a mattress full of strands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It quotes a ברייתא about what you may buy from a סורק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Loose מוכין (strands) left over from carding are presumed to belong to the customer, so buying them is buying stolen goods. If local custom gives them to the carder, they are his. A finished cushion or mattress is allowed everywhere; the reason comes in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: A carder, who combs out wool or cloth

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One may not buy strands from a carder,
because they are not his.
And in a place where the custom is that they are his, one may buy them.
And in every place one may buy from them
a cushion full of strands
and a mattress full of strands.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵין לוֹקְחִין מִן הַסּוֹרֵק מוֹכִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New ברייתא on the related topic of craftsmen and the customer's materials.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Loose strands from a carder are forbidden unless local custom gives them to him. A cushion or mattress stuffed with strands is permitted everywhere.

steps.title: Why is a stuffed cushion allowed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why a cushion or mattress full of strands may be bought everywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the last rule. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stuffing may also have come from customers' strands. So why is it allowed everywhere, even where loose strands are forbidden?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the last rule of step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a cushion or mattress stuffed with possibly stolen strands may be bought everywhere.

steps.title: He acquired the strands through a change
steps.stepSummary: By making the strands into a cushion or mattress, the carder changed them, and that change makes them his.
steps.simpleTranslation: He acquired them through a change.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. Turning the strands into stuffing changed them, so they now belong to the carder.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thief who changes the stolen item acquires it and only owes money to the owner. Loose strands are unchanged and still belong to the customer. Strands stuffed into a cushion have been changed, so buying them is no longer buying the customer's property.

keyTerms.meaning: A change in the item, which makes a stolen item the thief's own

steps.whatToRemember: Raw leftovers from a craftsman are forbidden to buy. Once he changes them into something new, they become his through שינוי and may be bought.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the key idea behind the next ברייתא about the weaver as well.

phrases.english: He acquired them through a change.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The carder acquired the strands through שינוי when he made them into a cushion or mattress.

steps.title: Leftovers you may not buy from a weaver
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists raw weaving leftovers that may not be bought from a גרדי (weaver).
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: One may not buy from a weaver wads, heddles, bobbin threads, or the leftover ends of spools.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new ברייתא about a weaver. It begins with a list of things you may not buy from him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are small, raw pieces of material from his work. Like the carder's loose strands, they are likely taken from customers' materials and are unchanged, so buying them is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Heddles, the loom threads that lift the warp

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One may not buy from a weaver
neither wads, nor heddles,
nor bobbin threads,
nor the leftovers of spools.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא, parallel to the carder ruling of step 11, now about a weaver.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Raw weaving leftovers may not be bought from a weaver.

steps.title: Finished items you may buy from a weaver
steps.stepSummary: The same ברייתא continues: you may buy from a weaver a spotted garment, weft and warp threads, spun thread, and woven cloth.
steps.simpleTranslation: But one may buy from them a spotted garment, weft and warp, spun thread, and woven cloth.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes by listing what you may buy from a weaver. This is the other side of the list in step 14.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These items have been worked into a new form: spun, set up as weft or warp, or woven. The ברייתא gives no reason, but this matches the idea of שינוי from step 13. Even if the materials once belonged to customers, they now belong to the weaver.
steps.whatToRemember: With both the carder and the weaver, raw leftovers are forbidden and changed or finished products are allowed.

phrases.english: But one may buy from them a spotted garment,
weft and warp,
spun thread, and woven cloth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא of step 14 with the permitted items.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Finished or changed items may be bought from a weaver.

steps.title: Why mention woven cloth if spun thread is already allowed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא of the weaver. If even spun thread may be bought, there is no need to say woven cloth may be bought.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: if you may already buy spun thread, do we really need to be told you may buy woven cloth?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that part of the ברייתא from step 15 seems unnecessary. Spinning is a small change, so weaving, which is a bigger change, should obviously be allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that a change made by the craftsman makes the material his. טווי (spun thread) has only a small change, so if that is enough, ארוג (woven cloth) has an even bigger change and should not need to be mentioned. The challenge is that the ברייתא appears to repeat itself.

keyTerms.meaning: They say; it introduces a question from the students of the בית מדרש
Now that; it sets up a 'this is already obvious' argument
Is it needed? Does it need to be said?

phrases.english: They say: Now that people may take spun thread,
is it necessary to say woven cloth?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the list in step 15 as repetitive
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's mention of woven cloth (step 15)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a small change (spinning) already makes the material the weaver's, a bigger change (weaving) obviously does too, so listing it is unnecessary.

steps.title: Woven here means twisted cords
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'woven' in the ברייתא does not mean full cloth. It means twisted cords, which are also only a small change.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'woven' mean? Twisted cords.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading the word 'woven' differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word does not mean cloth woven on a loom, which would be obvious. It means threads twisted into cords (תיכי), another kind of small change. So the ברייתא is teaching something new: this kind of small change is also enough to make the material the weaver's.

keyTerms.meaning: Twisted cords or chains of thread

phrases.english: What is meant by "woven"? Twisted cords.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining a term in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Woven' means full cloth, which would be obvious
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Woven' means twisted cords, a small change the ברייתא needed to mention

steps.title: What may and may not be bought from a dyer
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that test pieces, samples, and loose tufts of wool may not be bought from a dyer. A dyed garment, spun thread, and clothes may be bought.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: You may not buy from a dyer test pieces, samples, or loose tufts of wool. But you may buy from them a dyed garment, spun thread, and clothes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that applies the same idea to a צבע (dyer).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Small leftover pieces probably came from customers' wool, so buying them might mean buying stolen goods. Items the dyer has clearly changed, like spun thread or garments, are treated as his own and may be bought.

keyTerms.meaning: Test pieces, small bits of wool used to test a dye

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One may not buy from the dyer
neither test pieces nor samples
nor loose tufts of wool,
but one may buy from them
a dyed garment, spun thread, and clothes.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵין לוֹקְחִין מִן הַצַּבָּע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ברייתא about a different craftsman
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Small leftover pieces may not be bought from a dyer. Dyed garments, spun thread, and clothes may be bought.

steps.title: Why mention clothes if spun thread is already allowed?
steps.stepSummary: The same question is asked here: clothes are made from spun thread, so why list them?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that you may buy spun thread, do we need to be told about clothes?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same kind of question it asked in step 16, now about the dyer's ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Clothes are made from spun thread and have been changed even more. If spun thread is allowed, clothes are obviously allowed, so mentioning them seems extra.

phrases.english: Now that one may take spun thread,
is it necessary to say clothes?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the list in step 18 as repetitive
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Clothes are made of spun thread, so if spun thread is allowed, clothes obviously are too.

steps.title: Clothes here means felt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'clothes' means felt items, which are not made from spun thread.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'clothes' mean? Felt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by explaining which kind of clothes the ברייתא means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Felt is made from wool without spinning it into thread. So the permission for spun thread does not automatically cover felt, and the ברייתא had to mention it separately.

phrases.english: What is meant by "clothes"? Felt garments.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining a term in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Clothes' means ordinary garments made from spun thread
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Clothes' means felt, which is not made from spun thread
steps.whatToRemember: Both ברייתות (weaver and dyer) are read so that every item teaches something new: 'woven' means twisted cords, and 'clothes' means felt.

steps.title: Which leftovers from a tanner belong to whom
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that leather trimmings and pulled-off hairs belong to the owner of the hides. What comes off in the washing water belongs to the tanner.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If someone gives hides to a tanner, the trimmings and loose hairs belong to the owner. What comes up and washes off in the water belongs to the tanner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא, this time about an עבדן (tanner), sorting the leftovers between him and the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Trimmings and hairs are real pieces of the owner's hide, so they stay his. The stuff that floats off in the washing water is minor waste that the owner gives up, so the tanner may keep it.

keyTerms.meaning: A tanner, who processes animal hides into leather
The owner, the customer who gave the hides

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: One who gives hides to a tanner:
the trimmings and the loose hairs
these belong to the owner,
and what comes up and is washed off in the water
these belong to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another craftsman case in the same series
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Trimmings and hairs belong to the owner. What washes off in the water belongs to the tanner.

steps.title: The launderer's name hints at what he may keep
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה about black threads on a garment. רב יהודה makes a wordplay: the launderer is called קצרא, and he takes the 'short' (קצרא) bits.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'If it was black, etc.' רב יהודה said: He is called a קצרא, and he takes the קצרא (the short bits).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a launderer and brings רב יהודה's comment on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lets the launderer keep threads he pulls out in certain cases. רב יהודה links this to his Aramaic title, קצרא, which sounds like the word for short: he keeps the short bits of wool.

keyTerms.meaning: Short; the short shreds of wool
Etc.; it signals that the rest of the משנה is assumed

phrases.english: If it was black, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes our משנה: black threads on a white garment may all be taken by the launderer.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
He is called a 'katzara,' and he takes the short bits for himself.
phrases.notes: A play on words: the same letters mean 'launderer' and 'short.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה's case of the launderer
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The launderer keeps the short shreds, as hinted by his name.

steps.title: All threads count toward the measure for תכלת
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה teaches that all threads, even loose ones a launderer might remove, count toward the required distance for the תכלת hole. His son יצחק was strict and did not count on them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: All the threads count toward the measurement for תכלת. But my son יצחק is particular about them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a related teaching about these same loose threads and the measurement for ציצית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The hole for the ציצית must be a set distance from the edge of the garment. רב יהודה says even the loose threads at the edge count toward that distance. His son יצחק was stricter and made sure the measure was correct even without them.

keyTerms.meaning: The sky-blue wool used in ציצית
Count toward the required number or measurement

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
All the threads count toward the measurement for the sky-blue wool;
phrases.notes: This is the distance between the ציצית hole and the edge of the garment.

phrases.english: but Yitzchak, my son, is particular about them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: הַכֹּל עוֹלִין לְמִנְיַן תְּכֵלֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching from רב יהודה about the same loose threads
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Loose threads count toward the ציצית measurement, though יצחק was strict not to rely on them.
steps.whatToRemember: The same loose threads matter in two ways: who owns them (the launderer may take some), and whether they count for the ציצית measurement.

steps.title: How much thread counts as enough to sew with?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a tailor's leftover thread and asks what length counts as 'enough to sew.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: a tailor who left over thread, and so on. How much thread is 'enough to sew'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה and asks a basic measuring question. This sets up רב אסי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says leftover thread that is long enough to sew with goes back to the owner. It never says how long that is, so the גמרא asks for an exact amount.

keyTerms.meaning: And so on; the rest of the quote is not written out

phrases.english: A tailor who left over the thread, and so on.
phrases.notes: Some versions have 'מִן' in round brackets, and the corrected wording is 'אֶת' in square brackets. The meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: And how much is 'to sew'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the תכלת-thread discussion to the next line of the משנה, about the tailor.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The minimum length of leftover thread that counts as 'enough to sew with.'

steps.title: רב אסי: a needle's length outside the needle
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי gives the measure: a needle's length, outside the needle.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי said: the length of a needle, outside the needle.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אסי answers the question with a measure based on the needle itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The measure uses the needle as a ruler. The wording is short, though, and could be read in two ways. That opens the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The full length of a needle
Outside of, or beyond, the needle

phrases.english: Rav Asi said:
The length of a needle, outside the needle.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The thread must be a needle's length, outside the needle.

steps.title: What exactly did רב אסי mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: is it a needle's length plus another needle's length beyond it, or a needle's length plus any small extra amount?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: does it mean a needle's length, and beyond the needle another needle's length? Or maybe it means a needle's length, and beyond the needle any small amount?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is unsure how to read רב אסי's words, so it lays out two possible meanings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Option one: the thread must equal two needle-lengths. Option two: it only needs to be a little longer than one needle-length. This is a real difference in how much thread the tailor must return.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among them; they were unsure

phrases.english: They asked:

phrases.aramaic: מְלֹא מַחַט, וְחוּץ לַמַּחַט כִּמְלֹא מַחַט;
phrases.english: A needle's length, and beyond the needle the same as a needle's length;
or perhaps a needle's length,
and beyond the needle any small amount?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how to read רב אסי's answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'outside the needle' means another full needle-length or only a small extra amount.

steps.title: A ברייתא about short thread and small patches
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: thread too short to sew with, and a patch smaller than three by three, belong to the בעל הבית if he cares about them. If he does not care, they belong to the tailor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, as it was taught: a tailor who left over thread that is less than enough to sew with, or a patch less than three by three. If the בעל הבית cares about them, they belong to the בעל הבית. If the בעל הבית does not care about them, they belong to the tailor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to try to settle the question. This step only quotes the source; the reasoning from it comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא adds a new point. Even thread shorter than the 'sewing' length can belong to the owner if he cares about it. That means such short thread must still be good for something, and the גמרא will use this.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
A patch or scrap of cloth

phrases.english: Come and hear, as it was taught:
A tailor who left over the thread
less than enough to sew with,

phrases.aramaic: וּמַטְלֵית שֶׁהִיא פְּחוּתָה מִשָּׁלֹשׁ עַל שָׁלֹשׁ –
phrases.english: and a patch that is less than three by three –
when the owner cares about them,
they belong to the owner;
if the owner does not care about them,
they belong to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to try to answer the question of step 26.
steps.raayaObject: The meaning of רב אסי's measure.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא saying that thread shorter than the sewing length can still belong to an owner who cares about it.

steps.title: Reasoning from the ברייתא: what is the shorter thread good for?
steps.stepSummary: If the measure is two needle-lengths, shorter thread is still good for a loop, so an owner might care about it. If the measure is barely over one needle-length, shorter thread is useless, so why would he care?
steps.simpleTranslation: It works well if you say a needle's length plus another needle's length beyond it: thread shorter than that is still good for a loop. But if you say a needle's length plus any small amount, what is thread shorter than that good for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests both readings of רב אסי against the ברייתא and shows that only one of them fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא assumes thread below the 'sewing' length can still matter to the owner. Under the two-needle reading, a shorter thread can still make a loop. Under the 'tiny extra' reading, anything shorter is about one needle-length or less and is useless, so no owner would care about it.

keyTerms.meaning: It works well; it makes sense
A loop, or small loop stitch

phrases.english: It works well if you say a needle's length,
and beyond the needle the same as a needle's length –
less than this is good for a loop;
but if you say a needle's length,
and beyond the needle any small amount –
what is less than this good for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the proof out of the ברייתא quoted in step 27.
steps.raayaObject: That רב אסי means two needle-lengths.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's assumption that thread shorter than the sewing length still has a use.

steps.title: Conclusion: two needle-lengths
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that רב אסי meant a needle's length plus another full needle's length beyond it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, learn from this: a needle's length, and beyond the needle the same as a needle's length. Learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the question: the thread must be about two needle-lengths, and it confirms this with 'learn from this.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since only the two-needle reading makes sense of the ברייתא, that reading is accepted. The repeated 'learn from this' shows the proof stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Leftover thread goes back to the customer if it is at least two needle-lengths, a needle's length plus another beyond it. Shorter thread belongs to him only if he cares about it.

phrases.english: Rather, learn from this: a needle's length,
and beyond the needle the same as a needle's length.
Learn from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the result of the proof in step 28.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב אסי's measure means a needle's length plus another needle's length beyond the needle.

steps.title: A teaching contradicts the rule about the carpenter's adze chips
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says chips removed with a מעצד belong to the carpenter. A ברייתא says chips removed with a מעצד belong to the בעל הבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: what the carpenter removes, etc. But a ברייתא contradicts it: What a carpenter removes with a מעצד, and what is cut off with a saw, belong to the owner. What comes out from under a drill or a plane, and what is scraped off by the saw, belongs to the carpenter!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the opening words of the משנה about carpenters. Then it points out a ברייתא that seems to say the exact opposite about chips made with a מעצד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה gives מעצד chips to the carpenter and כשיל chips to the בעל הבית. The ברייתא gives מעצד chips to the בעל הבית. Both cannot be right, so the גמרא needs an answer.

keyTerms.meaning: And a contradiction was raised: another source seems to say the opposite
An adze, a cutting blade used to shape wood
A plane, a tool that shaves thin curls off wood

steps.confusionAlert: Keep the two sources straight. In our משנה, מעצד chips belong to the carpenter. In the ברייתא, מעצד chips belong to the בעל הבית. That clash is the whole question.

phrases.english: That which the carpenter, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה: what the carpenter removes with a מעצד is his, but what he removes with a כשיל belongs to the owner.

phrases.english: And a contradiction was raised: what the carpenter removes with an adze,
and what is cut off by a saw,
these belong to the owner.
But what comes out from under a drill
and from under a plane,
and what is scraped off by the saw,
these belong to him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the tailor's thread to the next case in the משנה, the carpenter.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that chips removed with a מעצד belong to the carpenter.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא rules that chips removed with a מעצד belong to the בעל הבית, which is the direct opposite.

steps.title: Different places used the word 'adze' for different tools
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that in the משנה's place there were two blades, a big כשיל and a small מעצד. In the ברייתא's place there was only one blade, and they called it מעצד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Where the תנא of our משנה lived, there were two blades. They called the big one כשיל and the small one מעצד. Where the תנא of the ברייתא lived, there was only one blade, and they called it מעצד.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the contradiction by showing that the two sources are using the same word for two different tools.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's 'מעצד' is really the big blade, which the משנה calls a כשיל. So both sources agree: big-blade chips belong to the בעל הבית, and small-blade chips belong to the carpenter. The argument was only about words, not about the law.

keyTerms.meaning: The תנא of the ברייתא, the outside teaching

steps.whatToRemember: There is no real disagreement. Big blade (כשיל, called מעצד in the ברייתא): chips go to the בעל הבית. Small blade (מעצד in the משנה): chips go to the carpenter.

phrases.english: Rava said: In the place of the tanna of our mishna
there are two blades.
The big one they call a "kashil" (ax),
and the small one they call a "ma'atzad" (adze).
In the place of the tanna of the baraita
there is only one,
and they call it a "ma'atzad."
phrases.notes: So the ברייתא's מעצד is really the big blade, the same tool the משנה calls a כשיל.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: בְּאַתְרָא דְּתַנָּא דִּידַן אִיכָּא תַּרְתֵּי חֲצִינֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different local meanings of the same word
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and the ברייתא argue about who owns מעצד chips.
steps.terutzMaskana: They mean different tools by 'מעצד', so they agree on the law.

steps.title: Stone chiselers, pruners and weeders: who keeps the scraps
steps.stepSummary: On the משנה's next line, the גמרא brings a ברייתא. Stone chips may be kept by the workers. Plant trimmings depend on whether the בעל הבית cares about them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: And if he was working at the owner's place, etc. The Rabbis taught: Stone chiselers are not doing robbery when they keep the chips. Those who prune trees, prune vines, trim shrubs, weed plants or hoe vegetables: when the owner cares about the trimmings, taking them is robbery. When the owner does not care about them, they belong to the worker.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה and brings a ברייתא with more cases of workers' leftover scraps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For stone chips, the ברייתא gives no condition: a worker who keeps them is never doing גזל. For plant trimmings, the rule depends on the owner. If he cares, taking them is גזל. If he does not care, the worker may keep them.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught, which opens a ברייתא
Stone chiselers who cut and shape stones
Those who prune or cut off branches

steps.whatToRemember: For plant trimmings, everything depends on the owner: if the בעל הבית cares, taking them is גזל; if he does not care, the worker may keep them.

phrases.english: And if he was working at, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה: if the carpenter works at the owner's place, even the sawdust belongs to the owner.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: Stone chiselers
are not doing robbery.
Those who prune trees, those who prune vines,
those who trim shrubs, those who weed plants,
and those who hoe vegetables:
when the owner cares about them,
taking them is robbery.
If the owner does not care about them,
these belong to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the משנה's next line and brings a related ברייתא about workers' scraps.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Stone chips may be kept by the workers. Plant trimmings are גזל if the owner cares and belong to the worker if he does not.

steps.title: Wild plants are free to take, unless local people care about them
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה rules that taking כשות and חזיז is not גזל. But in a place where people care about them, it is גזל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: Dodder and green grain are not subject to robbery. In a place where people care about them, they are subject to robbery.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה adds a rule about plants that grow in a field without the owner tending them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally owners do not care about these plants, so anyone may take them. But this uses the same idea as the ברייתא: once local owners do care, taking them becomes גזל. The rule follows the local custom.

keyTerms.meaning: Dodder, a wild plant (also used in brewing beer)
Green grain cut before it ripens, used as animal feed

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: Dodder and green grain
are not subject to robbery.
In a place where people care about them,
they are subject to robbery.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ברייתא's idea that 'it depends on whether the owner cares' for wild-growing plants.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Taking כשות and חזיז is not גזל, except in a place where people care about them.

steps.title: מתא מחסיא is a place where people care
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says the town of מתא מחסיא is a place where people care about these plants, so taking them there is גזל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: And the town of מחסיא is a place where people care.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא applies רב יהודה's rule to a real place, the town of מתא מחסיא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה made an exception for places where people care. רבינא tells us that מתא מחסיא is one of those places. So there, taking כשות and חזיז counts as גזל.

keyTerms.meaning: The town of מחסיא, a town in Babylonia

steps.whatToRemember: Whether wild plants may be taken depends on local custom. In מתא מחסיא people cared, so taking them there was גזל.

phrases.english: Ravina said: And the town of Mechasya
is a place where people care.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רב יהודה's exception to a specific town.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In מתא מחסיא, taking כשות and חזיז counts as גזל.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing הגוזל בתרא and finishing בבא קמא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא closes the last פרק, הגוזל בתרא, and announces that מסכת בבא קמא is complete.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, the last פרק called הגוזל, and with this, מסכת בבא קמא is finished.
steps.whatsHappening: This is not a new argument. It is the traditional closing line that marks the end of the פרק and of the whole מסכת בבא קמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words הדרן עלך are a promise to come back and learn this פרק again. The second half adds that this was the final פרק, so the entire מסכת is now complete. The discussion about what workers may keep, which ended with רבינא's statement about מתא מחסיא, was the last topic of the מסכת.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We will return to you.' The traditional closing said at the end of a פרק.
'The later הגוזל.' The name of the tenth and last פרק of בבא קמא.
'And it is finished.' Used to announce that a whole מסכת is complete.
'The First Gate.' The first of the three מסכתות about damages and money law.

steps.whatToRemember: This line closes both the last פרק, הגוזל בתרא, and the entire מסכת בבא קמא. The next learning in the series begins בבא מציעא.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up הגוזל בתרא with the earlier פרק הגוזל עצים. Both names start with הגוזל, so the word בתרא, 'the later one', tells you this is the last פרק.

phrases.english: We will return to you, the later perek 'HaGozel'
phrases.notes: There is also an earlier פרק that starts with הגוזל, so בתרא tells you this is the later one, the last פרק.

phrases.english: and Masechet Bava Kamma is finished

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ הַגּוֹזֵל בָּתְרָא וּסְלִיקָא לַהּ מַסֶּכֶת בָּבָא קַמָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Formally closes the פרק and the מסכת right after רבינא's ruling about מתא מחסיא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פרק הגוזל בתרא and all of מסכת בבא קמא are complete, with a promise to return and learn them again.
